title: Would you make this service stateless or stateful, and why?
summary: Probes whether you default to stateless reflexively, or can name the real cases — WebSocket gateways, in-memory session caches — where statefulness is the right call.

slides.markdown:
"Stateless" is the safe, expected answer in most system-design interviews — which is exactly why this question exists: to see if you'll say it reflexively even when it's wrong for the service being discussed. Some services, like a WebSocket gateway holding live connections, are genuinely better off stateful.

By the end of this topic you'll be able to default to stateless, but name the specific, concrete cases where statefulness is the correct trade-off instead.

slides.sectionTitle: Clarifying questions: live connection or per-request data only?
slides.markdown:
The deciding question: does this service hold a **live, ongoing connection** to the client (a WebSocket, a long-lived gRPC stream), or does it just process independent, one-off requests?

A service handling discrete HTTP requests almost always has no good reason to be stateful. A service holding an open connection has a much harder case for statelessness, since the connection itself *is* state that lives somewhere.

slides.sectionTitle: The answer skeleton: default stateless, justify stateful with a concrete reason
slides.markdown:
The skeleton: **start from stateless as the default**, since it gives trivial horizontal scaling and simple failover, and **only argue for stateful with a specific, named reason** — not "it's simpler" or "it's faster," but something like "this service holds an open WebSocket connection that has to live in one process's memory."

A candidate who states the default and then makes a real case for departing from it reads stronger than one who just picks whichever fits their existing diagram.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: a WebSocket gateway as the stateful counter-example
slides.markdown:
A **WebSocket connection-holding gateway** is the clearest legitimate stateful service: once a client connects, that connection is bound to one specific process's memory and socket table for its entire lifetime — there's no clean way to "move" an open TCP connection to another server mid-session.

This is genuinely different from a stateless REST endpoint, where any server can handle any request. Here, the server *is* the state, for as long as the connection is open.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: sticky sessions as a stateful compromise
slides.markdown:
**Sticky sessions** pin a given user to one specific server via the load balancer (using a cookie or the client's IP), letting an otherwise-stateless-looking service keep per-user data in local memory without an external store.

It's a compromise, not a clean solution: when that server dies or gets redeployed, every session pinned to it is lost or has to reconnect — you've reintroduced a small blast radius that full statelessness was designed to avoid.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: externalizing state to keep the app tier stateless
slides.markdown:
For most services, the better fix isn't sticky sessions — it's **externalizing the state** to Redis or a database, so any app node can read it. The app process itself stays disposable: it can crash, redeploy, or scale to zero without losing anything, because it never held the data of record in the first place.

This is why "stateless" services aren't stateless in the literal sense — they just push all persistent state to a store designed to hold it, instead of to their own process memory.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: stateless app tier with external state vs a stateful in-process gateway
slides.markdown:
![Side by side: a stateless app tier of interchangeable nodes reading and writing session state to an external Redis store, versus a stateful gateway tier where each node holds its own live connections with no external store](assets/stateless-vs-stateful.svg)

The left diagram's nodes are interchangeable — any one can serve any request. The right diagram's nodes are not — each holds connections the others don't have, which is exactly the property that makes it stateful.

slides.sectionTitle: The trade-off to name out loud: trivial scaling vs an extra network hop
slides.markdown:
| | Stateless (external store) | Stateful (in-process) |
|---|---|---|
| Horizontal scaling | Trivial — any node serves any request | Hard — connections/data pinned to specific nodes |
| Failover | Clean — a crashed node loses nothing of record | Costly — a crashed node's in-memory data or connections are gone |
| Per-request cost | Extra network hop to the external store, every time | No extra hop — data is already local |

**How to decide:** statelessness buys near-free horizontal scaling at the cost of a network round trip on every read; for a service with no live connection to hold, that trade almost always favors stateless.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: how do you scale the stateful version?
slides.markdown:
You don't scale a stateful gateway the way you scale a stateless tier — you **shard by connection identity**. Each gateway node owns a subset of connections (say, by hashing connection ID or user ID across nodes), and anything that needs to reach a specific connection has to route to the node that owns it, often via a lookup service or a consistent-hashing scheme.

This adds real complexity — routing, rebalancing when a node joins or leaves — that a stateless tier never has to deal with, and it's worth naming that cost when you propose it.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: a stateful node crashes — what happens to its connections?
slides.markdown:
Own this cost explicitly rather than glossing over it: every connection that node held is **gone**. Clients notice a dropped connection and must reconnect from scratch — re-authenticating, re-subscribing to whatever channel or topic they were on — to whichever node they land on next.

A well-designed client handles this with automatic reconnect-and-resubscribe logic, but the interview answer should state plainly that this is real, user-visible disruption, not something the architecture quietly absorbs.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: "always stateless" with no answer for real-time systems
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Always design services stateless" is a universal rule with no exceptions.

**Why it's wrong:** it collapses the moment a real-time system — a WebSocket gateway, a multiplayer game server, a live collaborative-editing backend — enters the conversation, since those genuinely can't avoid holding connection state somewhere in a process's memory. A candidate with no answer here looks like they memorized a rule instead of understanding why it usually holds.

**Correct model:** state statelessness as the strong default, then name the specific, real cases — live connections chief among them — where it doesn't apply, and how you'd scale that stateful case instead. See [sticky sessions and statelessness](sticky-sessions-and-statelessness) for the deeper mechanics of this trade-off.
